idiom_name: static nested UserBuilder with defaults, withEmail(...) returning this, build()
implementation_notes: Java's realization is the one the pattern was published with: a static nested UserBuilder holding a field per constructor parameter, defaults assigned in the field declarations, chainable withEmail(...) methods returning this, a static aUser() factory as the syntactic sugar, an optional but() that copies the builder to derive a similar object, and a build() that calls the product's constructor - kept private or package-private so tests cannot bypass it. Java records give a terse valid instance (plus a static validUser() factory) but no copy-with-modification syntax, so once a second or third field varies the override methods still have to be written by hand.
pitfalls: Builders are mutable accumulators: keeping one in a field or reusing an instance across tests leaks earlier overrides and produces order-dependent failures; start from aUser() in each test.
A builder calling a constructor that skips validation, or growing test-only setters, lets tests build objects production can never create, so the test stops proving anything about the real path.
Defaults now live in two places (builder and product); only the compile error at build() reliably reveals the drift when the constructor changes.

variants.name: Lombok @Builder-generated builder
variants.implementation_notes: Lombok generates exactly the hand-written API - builder(), per-field chainable setters, build() and optionally toBuilder() for the but() behaviour - so a team that already annotates its domain classes gets the pattern without maintaining it. Annotate defaults consistently with @Builder.Default (otherwise the builder starts at null/0 and ignores field initialisers) and use @Singular for collections; the generated API is invisible at run time but ties the builder to the annotation processor's view of the class.
pitfalls: Fields without @Builder.Default silently start at null/0 in the builder even when the class initialiser held a meaningful value - the classic trap that produces half-empty test data.
@Builder on one constructor documents only that constructor's API: a second constructor or a validating factory can be bypassed, so keep a single validating creation path.
